1:
Gill opens from where the previous chapter closed. Every part of the structure stood finished, Moses had surveyed both fabric and furniture, and all appeared executed exactly as prescribed. Henry seizes on what happens next. Materials had been inspected severally and approved; they must now be assembled. Yet although nothing remained undone, and although Israel was doubtless impatient to watch their sanctuary go up, Moses declined to raise a single board until an express word authorised him. It is good, Henry remarks, to see God going before us at every step. Clarke supplies the calendar entry: this command falls on the opening day of the opening month in the second year after their departure from Egypt.

An order of assembly follows, and Henry traces it through. First the dwelling itself, since God meant to inhabit and be served there; then the ark lodged inside with the veil drawn across it; then table, lampstand and incense-altar fixed outside that curtain, and a screen hung at the entrance. Afterwards the enclosure receives its brazen altar and its basin; and last of all rise the surrounding hangings, with a curtain for the gateway. Every item, Henry reckons, could be handled within a single day, since many hands were doubtless busy under Moses' direction.

Consecration waits until the placing is complete, and Henry refuses to treat that interval as accidental. Only when tabernacle and furnishings stood where they belonged was Moses told to hallow them with the compounded oil — a requirement issued long before but timed here. Nothing was sanctified until it occupied its proper station, because until then it was unfit for the purpose to which sanctifying devoted it. As everything is beautiful in its season, Henry writes, so is everything in its place.

Men are hallowed after objects, and a domestic picture carries the point. When goods arrive at a household they are marked first; only afterwards are servants engaged to carry the master's vessels, and such servants must be clean. Henry identifies the statute now enforced with one enacted earlier in the book, then reads the arrangement forward. Within the visible church, which is God's dwelling among mortals, ministers are equally requisite to guard the sanctuary's charge, and they too must receive their unction. Nor does the office stop with Aaron: it remained in his family until Christ arrived, and abides for ever in him who is the substance of all these shadows.

A closing observation concerns labour rather than joinery. Six months, by Henry's reckoning, sufficed to finish the whole undertaking. Where numbers give their hearts earnestly to a good cause, much may be accomplished quickly; and where divine commandments govern the workmanship throughout, everything will be accomplished well.
2:
Gill names the month and dates the interval. It is Nisan, as the Targum of Jonathan expresses it, the same month in which the children of Israel came out of Egypt, out of which they had now been a whole year excepting fourteen days. Wesley makes the same subtraction and adds two observations. The work was probably made ready just at the end of the year, so that appointing this day gave no delay, or next to none; and there is a precedent in Hezekiah's reign, when they began to sanctify the temple on the first day of the first month. The new moon, which by their computation opened every month, was kept with solemnity, so that this first new moon of the year was the more remarkable.

Clarke and Ellicott reckon the other way, from when the building started. Clarke takes it as generally supposed that the Israelites began about the sixth month after leaving Egypt and finished near the close of the first year, so that six months went into the making and the tabernacle stood erected one year all but fifteen days after the exodus. Such a building, he says, with such a profusion of curious and costly workmanship, was never got up in so short a time; but it was the work of the Lord, and the people did service as unto the Lord, for they had a mind to work. Ellicott arrives at nearly the same figure by counting the stages — they quitted Egypt on the fourteenth of Abib, reached the wilderness of Sinai in the third month, and the two long absences of Moses in the mount took up nearly three months with some days between them. It must therefore have been the sixth or seventh month before the work was commenced and the eleventh or twelfth before it was accomplished; and since the new year was approaching, its first day was naturally chosen as fittest for the inauguration. He corrects the title as he goes: not the tabernacle of the tent of the congregation but the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, the two words standing in apposition rather than in regimen.

Calvin refuses the premise on which all this computing rests. He cannot at all approve the opinion of those commentators who think the tabernacle was only now set up. It was complete in all its parts before Moses went the second time into the mount, as appears from the ark having then been prepared to receive the tables; and it had stood pitched outside the camp in token of divorce ever since the people made the calf. What the setting-up means, on his reading, is that it was fixed in its right and legitimate place — in the midst of the people, to whom it had been a stranger — and so brought back from its strange place to its proper one. That is why its solemn dedication is celebrated only after the renewal of the covenant, and why the anointing and the sacred oblations come with it, Aaron and his sons being consecrated at the same time.

Calvin finds his reading confirmed in the wording itself. Moses speaks of the tent of meeting as of something already well known, and had recorded that the name was given it by the mouth of God — which Calvin takes as evidence that this is the very tabernacle pitched at a distance from the camp. And he answers the obvious objection to the repetition of instructions already given. God repeats the same injunctions not because he distrusted the memory of his servant, but that it might be more fully apparent that he was himself the sole Author of the whole work, and that the work might obtain the more reverence, since he had so often deigned to give directions about it as concerning things of very great importance.
3:
The order of the furniture is commented on. Ellicott observes that the most precious of the objects the tabernacle was to contain goes in first and is then immediately covered with the veil; Gill describes it — the ark or chest where the law was, a testimony of the divine will, set in the most holy place.

At the table three notes converge. Gill identifies it as the table of shewbread, set in the holy place; Clarke reads the command to set in order the things upon it as placing the twelve loaves in the order described earlier in the book; Ellicott agrees that the twelve loaves are the things specially intended, and doubts whether the frankincense is also glanced at, since that may have been an addition to the earliest ritual. On the lamps he qualifies: the direction to light them need not mean at once, but at the close of the day.

Where the golden altar stood is a point the wording could mislead on, and both readers take the preposition the same way. Gill insists that setting it before the ark does not mean inside the most holy place, but over against it in the holy place. Ellicott says the same and locates it more exactly: outside the veil, though nearer to it than either the table or the candlestick. The hanging of the door he identifies as the curtain at the entrance.

Out in the court, placing is governed by practical fitness. Gill explains why the altar of burnt offering belonged in the open air: the people's sacrifices were brought there and offered by the priests, and the altar was properly set outside because of the smell and smoke. Ellicott gives the laver's reason: its place was close to the door, since the priests washed hands and feet there every time they set foot within. Gill closes with the court itself, which consisted of hangings on all four sides.

With everything in its place the anointing begins, and Gill gives its scope: the tabernacle and its vessels, the altar and its vessels, and the laver with its foot, all consecrated for divine use and service. Ellicott points back to the earlier legislation on both counts: the composition of the oil had already been prescribed, and at the same time the tabernacle, the ark, the table, the candlestick, the two altars, the laver and the sanctuary vessels had all been ordered consecrated by anointing.

Calvin will not let the oil be mistaken for the thing it stands for. There was no virtue or efficacy for sanctification in it, except so far as it was a type of the Spirit, from whom as its only source all holiness emanates; being a corruptible fluid it could not of itself avail unto spiritual service, though many passages of Scripture show it to have been a symbol of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The figure therefore teaches that nothing pleases God, and nothing is pure or holy in his sight, except what the Spirit's influence and grace has purged and duly consecrated. He adds a disciplinary purpose: God would have all the sanctuary's vessels set apart by this anointing from common use, so that Israel might distinguish between things sacred and profane, and that his service might receive due reverence, none intruding the pollutions of the flesh into a place marked out by that symbol.

One detail raises a question Calvin thinks worth answering. Why does the text give the altar of burnt offering a more exalted title, calling the tabernacle and its vessels simply holy but the altar most holy? He doubts not that it acquired the name from the sacrifices, which are themselves so called on account of the expiation made by them: Israel was thereby instructed that God is truly reconciled by holocausts and burnt offerings, since the holiness of holinesses resided on the altar itself.
12:
Gill states the purpose of bringing Aaron and his sons to the door: they were to be washed, anointed and clothed there, that they might minister in the priest's office. Ellicott notes that none of the three acts is new — ablution, investiture and anointing had all been appointed already as parts of the consecration service. Calvin, having expounded the garments and the mode of anointing elsewhere, asks his readers to hold two things in mind here. The first is a distinction of stages: Aaron had been appointed priest before, and is now at length inaugurated, so that he may begin the discharge of his office. The second is that the oil itself was consecrated by God.

From that second point Calvin turns sharply on his own contemporaries. It appears from it, he says, how foolishly the Popish bishops ape Moses when they sprinkle their priests and altars and other rubbish with stinking oil, since this ceremony of anointing, belonging to the ancient shadows of the Law, plainly ceased at the coming of Christ. He then borrows an observation from Augustine. Moses, who is commissioned to anoint the others, was never consecrated himself by any visible symbol — from which we may understand that outward signs are not to be estimated by the dignity of the minister but only by the ordinance of God; and further, that invisible grace has profited some without visible sacraments, whereas visible sanctification may be imparted and yet cannot profit without the invisible.

Two small corrections attach to the clothing and the order. Ellicott would render the garments given to the sons not coats but tunics; Gill observes that the sequence was fixed, Aaron anointed first and his sons after him.

The manner differed too, and Ellicott establishes it from the narrative in Leviticus. Aaron had the oil poured over his head; his sons were merely sprinkled with a mixture of oil and blood — a difference he takes to imply a lower degree of official holiness.

What an everlasting priesthood amounts to is the last question, and the answers agree in substance. Ellicott reports the Jewish commentators as maintaining that the single anointing of Aaron's sons sufficed for all time and was never repeated for any subsequent priest, who held the office fully without it; each high priest, on the contrary, was inducted into his office by anointing, which is why he came to be spoken of as the anointed priest. Wesley says the same more briefly: the unction sealed their priesthood for as long as the Jewish polity lasted and sufficed for all succeeding priests, none being anointed afterwards but the high priests.

Clarke carries the same fact forward until it runs out. By this anointing a right was given to Aaron and his family to be high priests among the Jews for ever, so that all born of that family had the priesthood without any repetition of the unction, enjoying it in their father's right; yet the high priest himself did receive the holy unction at his consecration, and that continued until the destruction of the first temple and the captivity. On the authority of Eusebius, Cyril of Jerusalem and others, Clarke holds that the custom went on among the Jews until the advent of our Lord, after which there is no evidence it was ever practised. He thinks the case worthy of observation. The Jewish high priest was a type of him who is called the high priest over the house of God, and when he came the functions of the other necessarily ceased; the sacrifices were never resumed after the destruction of the city and temple, since they hold it unlawful to sacrifice out of Jerusalem, and the unction ceased from that same period — because the true priest and the true sacrifice were come, and the types were no longer necessary after the manifestation of the antitype.
16:
Gill sums it in a line: Moses set up the tabernacle and every thing in its place, and anointed them, with Aaron and his sons. Ellicott is more careful with the timing: the verse states generally that Moses carried out the entire series of instructions, but tells us nothing about when; the passage that follows fixes the first set to the first day of the second year, while the narrative of Leviticus shows that the rest — the anointing and the consecration of the priests — were not executed until later. Henry keeps the same distinction in plainer terms: the rearing was a good day's work, the consecrating came some days after, and what we have here is that new-year's-day's work alone.

Where the work was done strikes Henry as an argument. When tabernacle and furniture were ready they did not put off rearing it till they came to Canaan, though they hoped to be there very shortly, but in obedience to God's will set it up in the midst of their camp in the wilderness. Those unsettled in the world, he warns, must not think this excuses their continued irreligion, as if it were enough to begin serving God when they begin to be settled. A tabernacle for God is a needful and profitable companion even in a wilderness — especially considering that our carcases may fall in that wilderness, and we may be fixed in another world before we come to fix in this.

What Moses did and how is where Henry and Calvin converge, both fastening on the same repeated formula. Henry observes that Moses not only did all God directed but did it in the order God appointed, for God will be sought in the due order; and that to each particular is added an express reference to the divine appointment, the words as the Lord commanded Moses recurring seven times in less than fourteen verses. Great as he was, Moses would not vary from the institution, neither adding to it nor diminishing from it in the least punctilio — from which Henry draws the rule that those who command others must remember that their Master also is in heaven.

Calvin presses the same observation into a polemic. It must be especially noted, he says, that Moses obeyed so as not to vary in the most trifling point from the form prescribed him, and that he so frequently enforces the fact that he did as God commanded — not without reason, for there is nothing to which men are more prone than mixing their own inventions with God's commands, as if they would be wiser than he. Moses insists on it so the people might know there was nothing of human invention in all the legal service. But if so great a prophet dared attempt nothing of himself in trifling matters, how great is the audacity of those who arbitrarily invent innumerable figments whereby God may be worshipped. Let us learn, Calvin concludes, to embrace with reverence whatever has proceeded from God, and reject whatever men advance of themselves.

How it went up so quickly is Ellicott's question, and he answers from the builders rather than the building. The tabernacle was constructed to be rapidly both put together and taken to pieces, the main difficulty lying in erecting the framework and stretching the fine linen and goats'-hair coverings upon it. But the family of Abraham had been familiar with tent life from the time it quitted Ur until the descent into Egypt, and its location there on the borders of the desert, near nomadic races, kept up that familiarity with tents, their structure, and the approved methods of pitching and striking them. It is not surprising, he concludes, that the first erection was completed in less than a day. Gill fixes the date: the first month of the second year of the departure out of Egypt.
18:
Gill enters a small qualification on the verb before anyone builds anything: Moses reared up the tabernacle not of himself, but with the help of others. Ellicott then takes the operation apart in the order the text gives it, and finds the whole stability of the structure resting on its first step. Everything depended almost entirely upon the sockets. They were of considerable weight, but they cannot by their mere weight have sustained the fabric in an upright position, and it is reasonable to suppose that they were let into the ground to a depth of some feet — which is why the erection necessarily commenced with fastening them. Once they were firmly fixed, the upright boards and the pillars were inserted into them by means of the tenons in which they terminated, and so stood erect; and the coupling by bars riveted the three walls into one firm and compact structure.

What was thrown over that frame is described three ways, and the three do not quite agree — the question being which of the verse's two clauses answers to which covering. Gill takes the tent spread abroad over the tabernacle to be the curtains of goats' hair. Clarke reads the same word more broadly: by the tent, here and in several other places, we are to understand the coverings made of rams' skins, goats' hair and the rest, which were thrown over the building, for the tabernacle had no other kind of roof. Ellicott separates the two terms the verse uses. What was erected was the wooden framework with its covering of goats' hair, and that is the true tent which roofed in the dwelling; the covering put above upon it is a distinct thing, the outer protection of rams' skins and seals' skins.

Keil and Delitzsch move ahead to what was placed inside once the frame stood, and stop on a single word. The testimony put into the ark does not mean the revelation so far as it already existed — so much of it, that is, as concerned the erection of the sanctuary and the institution of the priesthood — which is what Knobel arbitrarily supposes it to mean. It means the testimony proper: the decalogue written upon the two tables of stone, the ten words of the covenant, so that the term stands as an abbreviated expression for the tables of testimony. Only after the ark had been brought into the dwelling, they add, was the veil hung upon its hooks before it.
20:
What went into the ark is agreed, and Gill explains the name it goes by: the ten commands are called the testimony because they testified and declared what the will of God was with respect to things to be done and not done. Clarke identifies them plainly as the two tables on which the ten commandments had been written; Ellicott specifies further that these were the tables of stone written with the finger of God, which Moses had brought down with him from the top of Sinai on his last visit.

What else the ark may have held is where two of them part. Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan's claim that Moses put the broken pieces of the first tables in as well, and doubts it: what became of those fragments we nowhere read, and it does not appear that any tables were put into the ark except the ones Moses hewed by the order of God. Ellicott declines to argue from this verse either way — it is not proved by the passage, he says, that the ark held nothing but the testimony. On the staves he adds only that setting them on the ark means placing them in the rings, ready for use.

The arrangement of the outer room is described by Keil and Delitzsch as a plan with a centre and two sides. The table stood on the right, towards the north, with the shewbread laid upon it; the candlestick on the left, opposite the table; and the golden altar in front of the curtain, midway between the two sides but close to the curtain before the most holy place. When these had all been placed, the hanging was hung in the door of the dwelling. Ellicott fixes the two sides by the same reference point — the table on the right hand to one facing towards the veil, the candlestick directly opposite on the left — and adds a reason for the pairing that the plan alone would not give: the light would thus be thrown on the table of shewbread. He also suggests where the knowledge of these positions came from, since Moses may have known the right placing from the pattern that was shewed him in the mount.

How the loaves lay on that table draws a philological note. Gill has the twelve cakes of shewbread set in two rows, six in a row, and Ellicott agrees that they were arranged in two rows, as was afterwards commanded in Leviticus. Keil and Delitzsch object to the usual rendering of the Hebrew: the phrase does not signify a row of bread but the position or placing of bread, and the two rows are to be inferred from Leviticus and from the size of the table, two cubits long and one cubit broad.

Gill takes the trouble to say why the two altars are distinguished by their metals — the golden altar is so called because it was overlaid with gold, and to mark it off from the altar of burnt offering, which was covered with brass. Ellicott locates it by what stood beyond it: in front of the ark, the mercy-seat and the place assigned to the Divine presence, but separated from all three by the veil.

Who performed these acts is a point Gill will not pass over. Lighting the seven lamps was the business of Aaron and his sons; but they were not at present invested with their office, and so it was done by Moses, who in this and several other things mentioned in the chapter officiated as a priest. Ellicott enters a note on the hour rather than the man: the lamps were lit when the proper time came, that is, at even.
27:
Incense follows lamplight as the second sacerdotal act Moses performs, and Gill treats both alike: kindling and censing were functions he could never have ventured upon without express warrant from heaven. Ellicott binds the pair to a single hour — at evening, having trimmed and lit the lamps, Moses offered incense too, precisely as his instructions required.

Once nothing further remained to bring inside, the entrance was curtained. Gill notes why that step waits until this point in the narrative: the screen went up at the sanctuary's doorway only after everything destined for the interior had been carried in.

Outdoors, the brazen altar's position hangs on a particle that has dropped out of the Hebrew, and Ellicott argues for a specific restoration. Our translators assumed the missing word meant "at"; he judges it likelier to be the term employed a few verses earlier and rendered "before". On that reading the altar stood not against the doorway but facing it, at some remove. What was burnt upon it he identifies as Israel's first evening oblation — a lamb, accompanied by the meal offering appointed to go with it.

Between altar and tent the basin was placed, and both Gill and Ellicott refer its station back to the legislation that had already settled it. Keil and Delitzsch add the practical detail: water was poured in for washing, and the ablution bound Moses no less than Aaron and his family, being repeated whenever they entered the sanctuary or approached the altar.

That Moses should use a vessel designed for priests puzzles nobody but wants explaining, and Gill explains it. The basin belonged to the priesthood; Moses, discharging priestly duty, bathed there beside Aaron and his sons — men he was about to consecrate and induct by sacrificing on their behalf. Jarchi dates the episode to the eighth day of that induction. Gill also widens the clause about entering the tent: it prescribes not merely what happened on this occasion but perpetual practice thereafter.

The enclosure comes last, as the outermost thing naturally would. Gill supplies its measurements from the earlier chapter — a hundred cubits by fifty — and Ellicott refers both the curtains and their gateway screen to the same legislation. With those hangings ranged about dwelling and altar, and the entrance draped, Moses brought the whole undertaking to its end.
34:
Nobody doubts which cloud this was. Gill identifies it with the pillar that had gone before Israel almost from their coming out of Egypt, led them through the Red sea and on to Sinai, only now in a different form — not erect but more expanded, so as to cover the tabernacle outside. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the cloud, the same that directed their journeys from Succoth, and separates the verse's two halves: the cloud rested on the tent outside, while the glory, some ineffably brilliant appearance, entered within and filled the dwelling. It pleased God thus to declare his intention of keeping the promise to go with the people in person.

Clarke reads the event as a verdict on the work: God gave his approbation, and since the token was visible it signified to all the people that Jehovah was among them. He also marks a removal: the cloud had previously rested on the provisional tent Moses pitched outside the camp after the molten calf, but it now left that and settled on this one, made by God's command and direction — which Clarke believes stood at the centre of the camp, the twelve tribes pitching in order around it.

Henry, whom Wesley follows almost sentence for sentence, begins at creation. As when God had finished this earth, designed for man's habitation, he made man and put him in possession of it, so when Moses had finished the tabernacle, designed for God's dwelling among men, God came and took possession. By these tokens he testified both the return of his favour, forfeited by the golden calf, and his acceptance of all their expense and pains. God will dwell, Henry concludes, with those that prepare him a habitation: the broken and contrite heart, furnished for his service, shall be his rest for ever, and where God has a throne and altar in the soul there is a living temple.

The cloud itself Henry puts to four uses: a token of God's presence constantly visible, day and night, even in the remotest corners of the camp, so that they were inexcusable if they ever again asked whether the Lord was among them; a concealment, since God dwelt among them but dwelt in a cloud — whence Henry blesses God for the gospel, where we behold that glory as in a glass and not in a cloud; a protection, the best the tabernacle had, since they had sheltered it with covering upon covering but the cloud was its true guard; and a guide, resting while they rested and moving when they moved.

What filled the tent was fire and light, and Henry presses both its mercy and its terror. The curtains were no more singed than the bush had been consumed, for to those who have received the anointing the majesty of God is not destroying; yet the light so dazzled that Moses could not enter, but waited at the door until the splendour abated. What Moses could not do, our Lord Jesus has done, who as forerunner has for us entered and invites us to come boldly to the mercy-seat.

Calvin takes the sign as proof rather than ornament. The people knew by this pledge that the tabernacle had not been set up in vain, but that the earlier promise was fulfilled and this was the dwelling-place of the God who would be Leader and Keeper of his people; for it was not natural that a cloud should settle over the sanctuary, much less that cloud and fire should alternate perpetually by day and night. He notices a reversal in Moses' case: the cloud had once concealed him from the people, and its density now kept even him outside — from which their reverence ought to have grown, and by whose example, Calvin thinks, Levites and multitude alike were warned not to press further than allowed.
35:
Why Moses stood outside is answered twice over. Gill points out that he had been within already, in the holy place and the most holy, to see the furniture of each set as the Lord directed, and had come out again; now, with the cloud outside and the glory within, he was so struck with awe of the divine Being these symbolised that he could not engage his heart, or had not boldness, to go in until called. Ellicott reconstructs it differently: seeing the cloud descend as it had upon the temporary tent of meeting, Moses apparently tried to re-enter the tabernacle he had just quitted, and could not — the glory forbade approach, as it did the priests when it descended on Solomon's temple.

From the cloud's movements the whole march took its orders. Gill describes the manner: when the cloud was taken up by the Lord himself, or removed by his order, it rose and stood above the tabernacle in the form of a pillar and went before them. When it was not taken up they did not journey — and Gill draws a consequence easy to miss, for the cloud might rest two days, a month, or a year, as it probably sometimes did, which goes some way to account for the long continuance of Israel in the wilderness. Clarke refers the subject of these last three verses back to the pillar of cloud and fire at the exodus, treated at length there.

What was seen by night both Gill and Calvin explain as the same thing differently lit. Gill takes the phenomenon that appeared as a cloud in the daytime to have shone like fire in the night, or the fire to have been within the cloud, the same pillar which never departed from the people in the wilderness; and he gives its uses — a shelter from the sun by day and a direction of their way, the fire serving the same purpose by night, when in hot countries much travelling is done, and perhaps also terrifying wild beasts. Calvin says the same about the necessity of the change: by night a fiery column appeared, since the cloud would not have been visible amidst the darkness.

Calvin adds a second explanation and gets his best point from it. The thing happened not once or twice but in all their journeys, so that they were never without a sight of the witness of God's presence, whether it settled and commanded them to rest or ascended and gave the sign for removing the camp. It is the unevenness of that record which carried conviction. Had the cloud daily accomplished the same course, the very regularity would have obscured the power of God; but when for a whole year it did not move, and then frequently proceeded to a new place, pointing out now a longer journey and now a shorter, by that very diversity the paternal care of God, never unmindful of his people, manifested itself the more conspicuously.

Clarke carries the token as far as it went. The daily and nightly appearance was at once a merciful providence and a proof of the divinity of their religion, and continued throughout all their journeys, God never withdrawing it despite their repeated disobedience, until they came into the promised land. When the tabernacle became fixed, the Israelites having obtained their inheritance, this mark was no longer visible in the sight of all Israel but appears to have been confined to the holy of holies, resting upon the mercy-seat between the cherubim; and there it continued until the first temple was destroyed, after which it was no more seen in Israel till God was manifested in the flesh. He turns the whole to use before closing the book: these divine influences are necessary not for a time only but through all our journeys, through every changing scene of providence.
